comments.author: @ScottfromNB
comments.text: I grew up on the Bay of Fundy coast just west of Saint John at Duck Cove. Over 20 years from 1956 to 1976, I watched the edge of the gravel/sand bluff over Duck Cove recede over 20 feet, taking at least 5 summer homes over the cliff with it. Once down on the beach below, all evidence of them disappeared in a couple of years. Sadly, such locations, common on both the Bay of Fundy and the east coast of New Brunswick would've been a prime site for Indigenous settlements, even for the never located "Vineland" Viking settlement, possibly on the Gulf of St. Lawrence side of NB. Any evidence of them would be long gone like the summer homes that disappeared when I was a kid.

comments.author: @jayvallea
comments.text:
This documentary explores the rich, ancient human history of New Brunswick, which spans nearly 13,000 years. The film examines seven significant archaeological sites that provide evidence of Indigenous connection, trade, and settlement long before European contact. Many of these sites remain largely unknown to the general public, hidden beneath forests, urban infrastructure, or water.

Key sites discussed include:

The Augustine Mound (01:42 - 10:14): A 2,500-year-old burial site in Metepenagiag that revealed complex trade networks stretching to Lake Superior and the Ohio River Valley.
The Oxbow Site (10:14 - 16:28): An expansive site at the river's head of tide that preserves 3,000 years of continuous Mi’kmaq history through stratified flood deposits.
The Route 8 Campsite (16:28 - 21:37): An Ice Age site near Fredericton with an intact 12,700-year-old hearth, marking the oldest documented human occupation in the province.
Bentley Street (21:37 - 27:19): An ancient Wolastoqey portage corridor located near the Reversing Falls in Saint John, partially preserved beneath modern streets.
Teacher’s Cove (27:19 - 33:43): Shell middens in Passamaquoddy Bay that challenged historical assumptions about seasonal migration patterns.
Indian Beach (33:43 - 37:50): An important maritime site on Grand Manan used by the Peskotomuhkati for generations.
Mehtawtik (37:50 - 43:54): The principal village of the Wolastoqiyik, now submerged beneath the Mactaquac hydro-electric reservoir.
The documentary emphasizes that while these discoveries offer vital glimpses into the past, many other sites remain undocumented and are increasingly threatened by coastal erosion, industrial development, and flooding.
